Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-07 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom

Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), David (Redwood SE), Ibrahim (CSM), Priya (ArborSky SRE), Carlos (Head of Platform), Sofia (Product), Ethan (ML Eng)

Auto Summary (auto):
- Postmortem of a recent inference queue starvation incident that caused evictions and p99 spike on 2026-12-03.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay starting, thanks everyone for making time, we'll go through the incident timeline then mitigation options then next steps. if folks could say hi so we have them in the notes.
[00:08] Priya: hi, Priya here, SRE, thanks.
[00:11] Carlos: Carlos, head of platform.
[00:14] Sofia: Sofia from product.
[00:16] Ethan: Ethan, ML infra.
[00:18] David: David Kline SE, hi.
[00:20] Ibrahim: Ibrahim, CSM.
[00:22] Maya: cool, quick recap: on 12/03 you hit a sustained p99 latency spike for ~45 minutes during a heavy batch load — load pattern was an unusual mix of long context inference and many small chats which caused queue starvation and downstream evictions. Priya, please correct me if i m wrong on that.
[00:38] Priya: yeah that's right, the sequence lengths were bimodal, and our autoscaler didn't react because it was looking at average CPU not token queues. you saw a backlog in the inference-service queue, tokens kept piling until the runtime evicted some KV caches and that forced long tail rewarm which shot p99. the logs show a lot of "evictshun" messages - not sure why transcriber spelled that the other day but :)
[01:05] Ethan: to add, model kv cache evictions are expensive, rewarming adds ~200-400ms per affected request, when that hit a subset of shards we had amplification.
[01:15] David: i pulled the traces — we can see the interplay between scheduling window (30ms) and the batching logic, the continuous batcher tends to fold small requests into long-context batches and that starves small low-latency requests.
[01:28] Carlos: from our side the concern is SLA breach and customer impact. we saw downstream timeouts in our API and some error retries. we need both a fast short-term fix and a reliable playbook so on-call knows the knobs.
[01:40] Maya: agreed. ok let's talk mitigations. short term we proposed three things: 1) reduce max queue depth for long-context workers and reserve a lane for low-latency small chats; 2) set a soft backpressure threshold that shunts new small requests to a fallback model variant or to a degraded path; 3) tweak autoscaler to look at request queue length and p95 token wait in addition to cpu.
[02:05] Priya: can you explain the reserved lane idea a bit more?
[02:07] David: sure — essentially allocate N concurrent slots (e.g., 10% of workers or fixed number depending on capacity) that are only used for short context requests < 256 tokens. long-context requests use separate pools so they can't monopolize kv cache and batching behavior. it's like isolated hot path vs cold path.
[02:22] Priya: that sounds promising, but how hard is it to roll out on our private deployment? we run Redwood Private in our VPC with custom autoscaler.
[02:30] David: for Private it's a config change plus a small policy update in the router — we can give a config diff. runtime-side the serving engine already supports tag-based routing so it's mostly ops/config.
[02:41] Ibrahim: note for hosted customers we typically do this via model-routing policies and instance pools. we'll map that to your private setup.
[02:46] Carlos: cost question — reserving lanes reduces overall utilization, what is the expected cost delta?
[02:51] Maya: short answer: there's a small uplift. we'll model scenarios: 1) fixed reserved capacity (worse utilization) vs 2) elastic reserved burst with oversubscribe and fast fallback. i'll produce a cost delta estimate.
[03:03] Sofia: what about adjusting batching thresholds instead of splitting pools? maybe increase min batch timeout so small requests flush sooner.
[03:10] David: we can tune the continuous batcher. there are tradeoffs: lowering batch timeout reduces throughput efficiency but helps latency. combined with reserved lane it's safer.
[03:18] Ethan: also we noticed your eviction pattern correlated with a particular shard getting hot — there's some imbalance in request routing. we should look at shard distribution and affinity keys.
[03:27] Priya: i saw that; a small percentage of keys were getting many multi-turn flows. can we do shard-level fairness?
[03:31] David: yes, there's a couple of levers: round-robin routing with per-shard concurrency caps or a soft token bucket per-shard. we'll sketch both options.
[03:40] Carlos: operationally the big ask is: create an eviction runbook that oncall can follow in 10 minutes. what does that look like?
[03:47] Ibrahim: good framing. our suggestion: 1) triage script to detect queue-starvation signature (p95 tokens queued > X and evict count > Y); 2) immediate mitigation steps: reduce long-context worker queue depth, enable reserved-lane, flip fallback routing; 3) verification steps: run smoke queries to confirm latency; 4) rollback steps; 5) followup: capture sample traces and open a postmortem ticket.
[04:10] Priya: that triage script — can Redwood supply an example?
[04:12] David: yes we'll provide a minimal repro + triage script, it uses kinesis/batcher metrics and the runtime eviction counters. we'll attach in the doc.
[04:20] Sofia: for product we also want clearer SLOs around degraded outputs — e.g., do we accept fallback to smaller model with lower context? what are UX expectations?
[04:29] Maya: that's a good point — include a decision matrix in the playbook: severity vs fallbacks (e.g., severity 1 use degraded model X, severity 2 queue depth adjust, severity 3 escalate to SE).
[04:40] Carlos: any security/compliance implications if we change autoscaler or routing?
[04:43] Ibrahim: not really, config changes should go through your change control; no data plane change. we will document the config diffs and required approvals.
[04:51] Priya: one weird thing — during the incident some logs had auth token refresh failures coincidentally. not sure if related.
[04:56] David: could be secondary due to timeouts and retries. we'll look but likely not root cause.
[05:02] Ethan: re: verification metrics — suggest we add a canary harness that runs synthetic low-latency queries every 30s to detect queue starvation before users do. synthetic should sample small-context and long-context.
[05:14] Maya: good idea. we'll add that to the runbook.
[05:17] Priya: what's the risk of false positives? i worry about churn from canary alerts.
[05:21] David: tune with a short rolling window and correlation with eviction counters to reduce noise. also include auto-silence if known maintenance window.
[05:30] Carlos: timeline for changes — customer wants short term fixes in 1 week and full runbook + autoscaler tuning in 3 weeks. feasible?
[05:37] Maya: yes. short term config diffs and triage script within a week. full runbook and autoscaler policy tweaks in 3 weeks. we'll align dates in next_steps.
[05:45] Ibrahim: i'll own the runbook draft and will ask for review cycles.
[05:49] Priya: i can test the triage script and share traces.
[05:53] Sofia: product will sign off on fallback decision matrix.
[05:56] Maya: ok before we wrap — any blockers or concerns?
[05:59] Carlos: just need clarity on rollback and who has permission to flip the reserved-lane in our private cluster. also we need a dry-run plan.
[06:08] David: we'll include an explicit rollback and dry-run checklist in the doc; permissions should be your oncall + platform lead.
[06:15] Mia: (note: there was a brief call echo, transcriber imperfect)
[06:18] Maya: thanks everyone, recap: Redwood supplies eviction-playbook draft, triage script, repro, and cost delta; ArborSky supplies traces and test window. follow-up 30m call proposed 2026-12-14 to validate config changes.
[06:33] Priya: thanks all.
[06:35] Carlos: thanks.
[06:37] David: thanks, bye.
